issues.title: The registration-time canary is a FINDABILITY probe, not an importability probe — it cannot detect the exact failure mode the task measured
issues.detail:
`importlib.util.find_spec('escalation.submit')` locates the module's spec; it does NOT execute the module. The comment above it claims the process 'can prove the invariant here' and the warning text says '`escalation.submit` is NOT importable from %s'. Both overclaim.

Concretely: the MEASURED failure this whole task is built around is the third-party dependency floor — `escalation.submit` -> `escalation.queue` -> `shared.timestamps` -> `shared/__init__.py` -> `shared.async_sqlite_base` -> `import aiosqlite`. If `aiosqlite` (or any other transitive site-packages dep) is missing from sys.executable's environment, `find_spec('escalation.submit')` still returns a valid spec (the .py file is right there on disk), the canary stays silent, and the deferred child still dies on ImportError at fire time and files no L2 — precisely the 3404-class 'exactly one L2 must be filed on failure, got 0' outcome the canary exists to pre-empt.

The canary only catches the narrow case where the `escalation` package itself is absent from the interpreter — which is also the case least likely to occur, since this same process already imports `escalation.models`/`escalation.queue` at runtime in `_file_inprocess_escalation`.

Either actually import (`importlib.import_module('escalation.submit')` in a try/except ImportError — it is a one-time cost on a path that runs at most once per scheduled restart, and it is the same interpreter, so nothing is being simulated), or keep find_spec and correct the comment + warning wording to say what it actually proves ('cannot be located' rather than 'is NOT importable') and note the transitive-dep blind spot explicitly. The current wording will read to a future maintainer as a guarantee that does not exist.

issues.title: `--setenv=PYTHONPATH=` applies to the ENTIRE transient unit, not just the submit child — the deploy payload now runs with a PYTHONPATH it never had
issues.detail:
The token is placed on the systemd-run argv, so it is set for the whole `/bin/sh -c` payload — which is the deploy script, not just the on-failure `python -m escalation submit` branch. The docstring frames it as existing 'solely so the RP-4 `python -m escalation submit` child can import', but the scope is wider than that framing.

This is not hypothetical: the deterministic-runner detached path (deterministic_runner.py:_default_schedule_detached_restart) routes real deploy scripts through here with an EscalationSpec attached, and `scripts/restart-all-orchestrators.sh:215` invokes a bare PATH `python3 "$SCRIPT_DIR/drain_check.py"`. That interpreter (the system python3, not the workspace venv) will now start with `<repo>/escalation/src:<repo>/shared/src` — plus any ambient PYTHONPATH the orchestrator happened to carry — prepended to its sys.path. Today that is probably benign, but it is a cross-interpreter contamination surface that the change's own rationale does not intend and no test pins.

A strictly narrower form gets the same guarantee with no payload exposure: drop the systemd-run token and prefix the on-failure command inside the shell wrapper instead — `PYTHONPATH=<quoted roots> <python> -m escalation submit ...`. That keeps the env var scoped to the one process that needs it, keeps the non-escalation argv byte-identical exactly as today, and removes the need to reason about what else the transient unit runs.

issues.title: Under a real wheel install the resolved root is site-packages itself, which PYTHONPATH places AHEAD of the stdlib
issues.detail:
`Path(loc).resolve().parent` for a wheel-installed `escalation` resolves to `<venv>/lib/pythonX.Y/site-packages`. The docstring explicitly claims this 'keeps this correct under both the editable install used in the deployed venv and a real wheel install'.

It is not equivalent in the wheel case. PYTHONPATH entries are inserted into sys.path BEFORE the stdlib directories, whereas site-packages normally sits after them. Putting site-packages on PYTHONPATH therefore inverts stdlib-vs-site-packages precedence for the child, so any site-packages distribution shipping a top-level module that shadows a stdlib name would win where it previously lost.

The deployed environment is editable, so this is latent rather than live — but the docstring asserts the wheel case is covered, and it is the docstring a future maintainer will trust when the deployment changes. Either skip roots that are already on the child's default sys.path (a `site.getsitepackages()`/`sysconfig.get_paths()['purelib']` filter), or narrow the claim.

issues.title: `test_partial_resolution_still_emits_what_resolved` silently assumes `escalation` and `shared` resolve to DIFFERENT roots
issues.detail:
The negative assertion `not any((Path(r) / 'shared' / '__init__.py').exists() for r in roots)` — described in-test as 'guards the stub itself' — only holds because the editable install gives `<repo>/escalation/src` and `<repo>/shared/src` as distinct roots. Under a wheel install both packages resolve to the same site-packages root, so the `escalation` root would also contain `shared/__init__.py` and this assertion fails even though the code under test behaved correctly.

Same environment coupling applies (less sharply) to the positive filesystem assertions in `test_setenv_pythonpath_present_and_carries_resolvable_roots`. Consider asserting against `importlib.util.find_spec(...)`-derived expected roots rather than probing the filesystem for sibling package layout, so the cells pin the FUNCTION's contract rather than the current install mode.

issues.title: A sibling test in the same file still pins fixed argv offsets 7/8 and was left unconverted
issues.detail:
`test_schedule_detached_systemd_restart_without_escalation_builds_unbranched_wrapper` still does `assert argv[7] == '-c'` / `wrapped = argv[8]`. It passes today only because it exercises the `on_failure_escalation=None` path where no `--setenv` token is spliced in — i.e. it is correct by accident of which branch it happens to test, not by construction.

The diff converted the two offset-based assertions it had to touch to the index-derived `sh_at = argv.index('/bin/sh')` form and documented why. Leaving this third one behind means the next person adding a systemd-run option gated differently gets a confusing partial-failure. Convert it for the same reason the other two were converted.

issues.title: Ambient PYTHONPATH entries are forwarded verbatim, so a relative entry silently re-anchors to the child's cwd
issues.detail:
Entries from the parent's `PYTHONPATH` are `_add`ed as-is, while the resolved roots go through `Path(loc).resolve()`. A relative ambient entry (`.`, `src`, `../shared/src`) would therefore be re-interpreted by the child against `--working-directory=<self.cwd>` rather than against the orchestrator's own cwd — a different directory in general, and exactly the class of implicit-cwd bug RP-3 exists to close.

The new test explicitly `monkeypatch.delenv('PYTHONPATH')` before asserting every root is absolute, so the absoluteness invariant it pins does not actually cover the ambient-entry path (the sentinel used in the propagation test is itself absolute). Resolving ambient entries too — or at minimum dropping/warning on relative ones — would make the emitted value uniformly cwd-independent, which is what the docstring's 'the deferred unit runs under the systemd user manager, not this process' reasoning implies.

issues.title: `_detached_plan_with_spec` takes an unused `tmp_queue_dir` parameter
issues.detail: The helper's first parameter is never referenced in its body — the queue dir only reaches the plan via the already-built `spec`. Every call site therefore threads a value that does nothing, which reads as if plan construction depends on the queue dir when it does not. Drop the parameter.

verdict.summary:
The change is well-motivated and the core mechanism is sound: `systemd-run --user` genuinely propagates none of the caller's environment, so a deferred RP-4 `python -m escalation submit` child needs its import roots supplied explicitly on the argv, and building them from this process's own `find_spec` resolution (rather than a hardcoded repo layout) is the right call. Gating the token on `on_failure_escalation` correctly keeps the no-escalation argv byte-identical, the loud-over-silent degradation path never blocks the restart (verified by the new dispositions asserts), and the two fixed-offset argv assertions that the new token would have broken were converted to index-derived form rather than re-hardcoded. I ran orchestrator/tests/test_proc_supervision.py + test_service_restart.py (111 passed) and test_deterministic_runner.py + test_supervision_composition_integration_gate.py (293 passed) — all green, and I confirmed deterministic_runner already delegates to RestartPlan so there is no second copy of the argv builder left unpatched.

Two findings are worth acting on before this lands. First, the registration-time canary does not prove what its comment and warning text say it proves: `find_spec('escalation.submit')` locates a module without executing it, so the specific MEASURED failure mode driving this task — a missing site-packages dep such as `aiosqlite` reached transitively via `shared/__init__.py` — passes the canary silently and still files no L2 at fire time. Either import for real or narrow the claim. Second, `--setenv=PYTHONPATH=` is scoped to the whole transient unit, not the submit child the docstring says it exists 'solely' for; the deploy payload shares it, and `scripts/restart-all-orchestrators.sh` invokes a bare PATH `python3 drain_check.py` that will now start with repo src roots prepended. Prefixing the on-failure command inside the shell wrapper instead gets the identical guarantee with no payload exposure. The remaining five findings are lower-stakes: a wheel-install stdlib-precedence hazard the docstring claims is covered, two tests coupled to the current editable-install layout, one sibling test left on fixed offsets, unresolved relative ambient PYTHONPATH entries, and an unused helper parameter.
